title: Chapter 133 – The Stored Copy
html:
[Western Basin – Lin Jian]

The fourth Operator was a cheerful man, and it is the worst thing about him.

Jian understands this on the second morning, under the cold blue lamp, with the second page of the log lying open on the desk and a cup of Lan Ji's bitter tea at his elbow. The page is a joke. A long, rambling, affectionate joke about a goat that had eaten the school's only copy of the alphabet. It is signed with a small drawing of a smiling face, and below it, in the same quick hand, a note: Day 2. I have decided to be happy. It is an experiment. Please do not interfere.

He reads it three times. He finds, to his shame, that he is smiling.

"He does that," says Lan Ji, from the door. She has brought bread and a bowl of lentils, and she sets them on the corner of the desk without looking at the page. "My teacher said the same. He said the old man could not bear to be sad in front of children, and so he made himself funny, and after a while it was true." Her mouth quirks. "He wrote a hundred and twelve songs about vegetables."

"Did you sing them?"

"Every spring. At the planting." She pauses. "I am very sorry. They are not good songs."

So he reads, one page a day, in the blue light, and the days go by.

He had expected grief. What he finds is a school. He watches it grow, a few lines at a time, from nine frightened survivors in a ruin of glass to forty, to a hundred, to two hundred. A man in his thirties sits on a bench in the sun and teaches a child to read by tracing letters in the dust. He builds the first house with his own hands. He invents a loom. He learns the names of every goat. He writes about the Basin at night, the murmur of the city beneath the glass, as the loveliest thing he has ever known. I lay on the plain for six hours, he writes on Day 6. A woman was singing. I do not know the song. I think I will never forget it.

The next line is crossed out, with a single firm stroke. Jian holds the page up to the lamp. Under the ink, faint but legible:

And that is the trouble.

* * *

On the ninth day, a child falls in the well.

It is not in the log. Lan Ji tells him at supper, in the long hall, under the glow of the obsidian lamps, in the matter-of-fact way of a woman reporting the weather. A boy of six, called Dun, had been playing at the rim, and slipped, and went down thirty feet into black water. Half the school ran to the well. Nobody could reach him.

"What happened?"

"Pebble," says Lan Ji.

He turns his head. The little gray beast is curled on a bench by the fire with a sleepy, self-satisfied air, and a bowl of milk at her feet.

"She heard him," says the reader. "Before any of us. She woke from sleep and ran out the door, and stood at the well's edge, and said in a voice that carried across the whole yard, there is a seam in the bottom, left of the third stone. We lowered a rope. The boy was clinging to it." She shakes her head. "Nobody had told her the well was dangerous. Nobody had said a word."

"I did not hear her go."

"You were asleep. She did not wish to wake you." Lan Ji lifts her bowl. "Dun is alive. His mother has been trying to give her a goose all day."

"Did she accept it?"

"She said geese are loud." A flicker of humor crosses the reader's calm face. "She accepted a pie."

Pebble opens one eye. "It was a very good pie," she says.

He laughs. It is the second time that month. When he lies down that night on the cot in the guest-house, with the bell on its red thread chiming faintly as the little beast turns over in her sleep, he finds himself looking at the ceiling and thinking, absurdly, of Qinghe. Eat properly, she had written. He has been eating very well.

* * *

In the afternoons he works for the school, because he cannot sit still.

The great loom in the weaving shed has a cracked beam, and he mends it with a dowel and a wedge of seasoned ash, while two dozen small girls watch with their chins on their fists. The mill-wheel on the stream is out of true; he corrects it with a sledge and a level. A boy of ten brings him a broken flute. A woman brings him a pair of spectacles with one cracked lens. Every night he earns his two units, and every night the cell at his belt tops itself up to twelve and the surplus drains away like water from a stopped basin. He no longer minds. It has become a kind of prayer.

"You do that as though you have done it all your life," says an old man, watching him bind a split axle.

"I have done it for about forty years."

"Then you have done it all your life." The old man grins toothlessly. "The fourth did the same. He could not pass a broken thing without his hands itching. The children called him the Mender. They put it on his stone."

Jian ties off the cord. The axle is sound. He sets it down, and for a moment he looks at his own hands, at the callus on the thumb, the pale old scar across the left palm that every Operator has borne.

It is a good scar. It has healed clean.

"Did he ever mend anything he could not fix?" he asks.

The old man considers. "A heart, once," he says. "A widow's. He did not do it on purpose." He spits in the dust. "Do not tell the reader. She would be scandalized."

* * *

Day 14. A visitor.

She came to the school on the sixth of the month, the way the dust comes, quietly, without any warning. A woman in a plum-colored veil, with a book under her arm. I knew her at once, though I had never seen her. She stood at the edge of the glass in the heat and did not come in. She sent a child to ask if I would speak with her.

I said yes. I said it to be polite.

She told me she was the Keeper of the Roll, and that her name was Tuo Xiangyi, and that she had come twenty years to find me. She told me the Order had served the Operators for six hundred years. She told me, very gently, that I did not have to go through the Gate.

I was so surprised that I laughed. I told her I had decided that already.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "I know. That is why I came. I wished to tell you what it will do."

I said, "What will it do?"

She said, "It will be done anyway."

Jian lays the page down. He sits very still with his hands flat on the desk.

It will be done anyway.

On the shelf behind him, a thousand glass tablets glow with faint blue fire. He can feel them like eyes. In the corner, the toy horse stands on its ledge, three-legged, patient, forever on the point of trotting out of the room.

He turns the page over, and the next, though he is not supposed to. The Dock does not allow it. The paper is blank. He closes his eyes and presses the heels of his hands to them, and lets the dark come, and the words with it. It will be done anyway. He thinks of Qin Hao's stone hands. He thinks of Sang Ruo's hooked character, remain, and a name fading from a book.

She was ashamed, Pebble had said, of the Keeper at Sunken Lamp. They are all very polite.

Perhaps that is what shame is, he thinks. A thing that is done anyway.

* * *

Day 21. I have asked the Clerk.

I have not asked before. I was afraid. For twenty years I have lived with a voice in my head that says READY and STEP and HOME, and I have treated it like a servant in a house, to be given orders and otherwise ignored. But today I sat down at the desk with the lamp lit and said, aloud, "I want to talk."

It said, "TALK."

I said, "Is the Gate a door?"

It said, "NO."

I said, "What is it?"

It said, "A DOOR HAS TWO SIDES. THE GATE HAS ONE SURFACE. IT IS A COPYING SURFACE."

I did not know what that meant. I asked it to explain. It said, "PLACE A PAGE ON THE SURFACE. THE PAGE IS COPIED. THE ORIGINAL IS NOT MOVED. A SECOND PAGE APPEARS, ELSEWHERE."

I said, "I am not a page."

It said, "YOU ARE A PAGE."

Jian opens his eyes.

There is no sound in the room, but the lamp seems brighter, and the air thinner. He reads the passage again. His heart is beating slowly and hard.

"A page," he says aloud.

He has not meant to speak. The Dock hears. On the wall above the desk, a faint line of text appears, pale gold on the green stone, for the first time since he arrived.

```
LAN TONG — ARK-4 CHANNEL
Query received: "a page"
Answer 3 of 3 (home):
A copying surface does not move the thing it copies.
The Operator was copied. One copy was placed here.
The other was kept.
The kept copy is HOME. It is not a place.
It is a record, held in a first world that
needed a record. It sleeps.
The copy placed here is the WORKING COPY.
The working copy is not meant to return.
The working copy is meant to be RESTORED OVER.
```

Restored over.

He reads the line twice. Then, because his hands have started to shake, he lays them flat on the desk and holds them there.

* * *

He walks out onto the glass at dusk, alone, and stands in the middle of it for an hour.

The sky is violet, the stars just beginning. The plain around him is a sheet of dull gold, utterly still. Somewhere beneath his feet, seven thousand people murmur and laugh, and a bell rings, and a man says careful, that's hot. The Unkept are a line of gray shapes at the rim. The Nameless is nearest, forty paces behind, and has not moved.

He does not weep. He has the odd sense that he has done all his weeping already, in the tent, in the avalanche, over an old man's death, and that what is left is something colder and clearer.

The working copy is meant to be restored over.

He had thought of the Gate as a choice. A door he might go through or refuse. The Cole door in his soul, the Chain on the ridge, the three stones, the House, the Order, the Registry: all of them parts of a great patient machine, each with its own small voice saying home. He had understood home as the place Ethan Cole came from. He had understood the loop as a story of a man, sent again and again into the same cage.

He had never understood it as a story of the cage's inhabitants.

Lin Jian was born in the Orchard. He weighed like a stone in a sack. He did not cry. His father held him in the crook of one arm and said, Well, little stone, you'll sink us all. He grew up in a garden. He learned his letters from a mother who counted the days on her fingers. He was an apprentice, a gatekeeper, a son, a brother. He has done a great many things in thirty-eight years, some of them well. He has a sister who keeps a ledger of doors.

The working copy is meant to be restored over.

"Pebble," he says.

She is on his shoulder. She has been there the whole time, silent.

"Is it true?"

She does not answer at once. When she does, her voice is very small.

"I cannot hear a lie in it," she says. "I have tried. There is no seam. It is a smooth wall, all the way down." She presses her face against his ear. "I am so sorry, Jian."

* * *

The Unkept come to Lan Ji on the twenty-ninth evening, in a body, and stand at the door of the long hall in a row.

She is eating. She sets down her spoon, wipes her hands, and rises. She has the manner of a woman who has been waiting for a delegation her whole life. The man with the white eye is at their head. He has not spoken since the Pass. His cracked lips work, and nothing comes.

"They wish to hear the glass," Jian says, from the bench by the fire. "I think. They want to know whether their names are in it."

"I know what they want." Lan Ji's face is grave. "It is a thing the school does for the dead. We have never done it for the living. I do not know that it is right." She looks along the line of ragged men. "It may hurt. When a name comes back to a person who has lost it, it does not come gently."

The white-eyed man bows his head.

She takes them out onto the plain. It is dusk. The glass is dull copper. She makes them lie down in a row, fourteen of them, on their backs, with their ears to the polished surface, and she kneels beside the first and lays her palm on his brow. "Listen," she says. "Listen for the one that is yours. It will be the one that sounds like a hook in the throat."

Silence. The wind drops. A long time passes. Jian stands at the rim with his arms folded, and Pebble on his shoulder, and the Nameless a little apart.

Then, from the end of the row, from the third man, there rises a sound that is not a word at all. A cracked, helpless, enormous cry, like an animal waking. The man sits bolt upright. His face is working. He is clawing at his own collar, at the dull tag hung there, and tearing it away.

"Ma," he says. "Ma. Ma. That was her. That was what she called me."

"What?" says Lan Ji, very gently. "What did she call you?"

"Shuang." He is sobbing. "I was Shuang. I had a mother. I had a mother."

One by one, over the next hour, three more of them find it. A single syllable each. A scrap, a nickname, a pet word from a long-dead kitchen. They weep. They embrace. They fall silent. The white-eyed man is not among them. He lies on his back with his hands open and his one good eye wide to the stars, listening, listening, and the glass gives him nothing.

When the stars are out he sits up and says, in his rusty voice, "It is all right. Mine was a long time ago."

"I am sorry," says Lan Ji.

"Do not be." His smile is crooked. "Four of fourteen. It is more than I had."

Jian turns away. He does not want them to see his face.

* * *

Day 33. I did not sleep.

I have asked the Clerk the question I should have asked on the first day. I asked, "What happens to the person who was here before I arrived?"

It said, "THERE WAS NO PERSON."

I said, "There must have been. The body was born. Someone was in it."

It said, "THE BODY WAS BORN. THE PERSON WAS GROWN. THE WORKING COPY DOES NOT ARRIVE AT AGE TWENTY. IT ARRIVES AT BIRTH. IT IS PLACED IN A CHILD WHO IS EXPECTED. IT GROWS. IT FORGETS. IT BECOMES THE CHILD."

I said, "And when I go through the Gate?"

It said, "THE WORKING COPY IS RESTORED OVER. THE CHILD IS NO LONGER THERE."

I said, "He is me."

It said, "HE IS THE CHILD."

I have been sitting at this desk for four hours. I have written the sentence six times and crossed it out six times. I am going to leave it standing. I want whoever reads this to understand that I did not expect to feel it, and I feel it more than I have ever felt anything.

They are different. We are different. I was born a man in a lab and I will die a man in a bed, and somewhere in the first world is a man who sleeps. But the child who was placed in this body, who learned his letters on his mother's knee and ate his mother's soup and was loved, that child grew up in these years without me, and I do not know who he is. I only know he is not the one who sits at this desk.

And that when the Gate opens, he will be gone.

Jian reads the page standing. He cannot sit.

He reads it again. His mouth is dry. A line runs through the middle of his chest, from the breastbone out, thin and bright and cold, and he knows with perfect calm that it is the Cole door, aching, like a bruise.

I have been Ethan Cole for thirty-eight years, he thinks. I have been Lin Jian for thirty-eight years.

He does not know which sentence is true. He suspects it is both. He suspects the whole machine was built to make that impossible to tell.

* * *

Lan Ji finds him at the foot of the library stair on the thirty-eighth night.

He is sitting on the bottom step in the dark, with his hands between his knees. She stands over him for a moment. Then she lowers herself, unhurried, onto the step beside him, with her staff across her lap, and says nothing at all.

They sit together for a long time. The school is quiet. A goat bleats, far off. Behind them in the Dock the blue lamp burns, and the thousand tablets glow, and the dust lies in its peaceful skin.

"My teacher had a saying," says Lan Ji at last. "When a man does not know what to do, let him be useful."

"I have tried that."

"Did it work?"

"It worked for ten years." He almost smiles. "It is a very good saying."

"It is a very small one." She turns the staff in her hands. "He also said, near the end, that the old man had told him a thing. Something that was not in the log. The fourth Operator said it on the night he died, when the two strangers were sitting in the corner with their veils down." Her voice is steady. "He said that he had asked the Clerk one last question. A question he had not dared to write."

"What was it?"

"He asked whether the child was happy." She looks at Jian. "And the Clerk said, THE CHILD IS NOT RECORDED. THE CHILD DOES NOT EXIST IN THE STORED COPY."

Jian is silent.

"And the old man laughed," says Lan Ji. "My teacher said it was the most terrible sound he ever heard. And then he said, Then I have to be the one to remember him."

She rises, stiffly, and leans on her staff.

"I do not know what you are going to do," she says. "I know only that someone must be the one to remember. If you cannot, there are two hundred and nine of us who will try."

* * *

The bell rings on the thirty-ninth night, when he is asleep.

It is a tiny thing, a silver trill, and it is Pebble who wakes first. She is at the window in an instant, ears flat. He sits up in the dark. For a moment he cannot think what has happened. Then the little bell on its red thread shivers again, and a second chime answers, from very far away, thin and urgent and frightened.

Pebble listens with her eyes shut.

"It is Yue," she says. "She is not saying hello."

"What is she saying?"

"Mother has fallen." The little beast's voice is very quiet. "Not badly. In the kitchen. She was reaching for a pot. She says she is well, she says she was only dizzy, but Bai has looked at her and Bai's hands were shaking." A pause. "She says Mother's breath is thin. Thinner than it was. She says the Foundation pill is a year too late if we wait another winter."

Jian is already pulling on his boots.

"And Bai?"

"Bai is ninety-three." The bell chimes again, softly, a long falling note. "She says he is cheerful. He told her he would make the pill if it killed him." Pebble opens her eyes. "She says that was not a joke."

He stands in the dark with one boot in his hand. The Seal is at sixty percent. The Reservoir is full at the other end of the world. A year in a room. A page a day. A cold blue lamp.

A man cannot be in two places, he thinks. But a seam can.

"Tell her I am coming," he says.

"It is three thousand li."

"Tell her anyway."

Pebble lifts a paw. The bell rings once, clear and bright, a single note into the dark. And across the endless night, across a continent of ice and glass and desert, a small cold voice answers: yes.

* * *

Day 40. This is the last page.

I am seventy-one and my hands shake. The Keeper is waiting outside. I can hear her breathing. The children are asleep, and I have kissed each of them, and the school is quiet. I have a bowl of water by the bed and a letter to write.

Lin Jian,

I do not know what you will decide. I did not decide anything. I refused, and I stayed, and I was happy, and none of it mattered, because when a working copy dies the Gate restores over it anyway. The Order will carry you there. They do it gently. It is not cruelty; it is a mercy. They believe you will wake in a white room and be glad.

I think they are right. I think I will be glad. I think that is the worst of it.

Here is what I learned in forty years that I could not write until now:

The Gate has a hinge. It is the third stone. The first two seat the lock and the key. The third seats the door. The door is what makes the Gate go both ways.

It is not a mistake that you were built to wait for it. It is not a mistake that the Chain was built to wait for you. Somebody wanted the eighth Operator to complete the Gate. Somebody wanted the Gate to go both ways.

Ask yourself what a Gate that goes both ways is for.

And ask yourself who is waiting on the other side.

—E.C. (fourth)

Beneath it, in dark fresh ink, in the sharp hand he has come to dread:

I'm sorry.

—E.C.

He sits with the page in his lap. The lamp burns blue. The little horse watches from its ledge.

On the wall above the desk, the pale gold letters have not faded.

```
RESTORE POINT: ETHAN COLE (stored copy)
WORKING COPY: LIN JIAN
ON RESTORE: WORKING COPY RELEASED.
Seal: 60% — Cole door: OPEN (Page 2 ready)
```

Released.

He reads the word until it stops looking like a word.

Behind the shelves of glass, in the narrow gap beside the cot, the seam is exactly where the fifth Operator said it would be. He takes one step, four units, one more small coin from the drawer, and comes back with the fourth jar in his arms: squat, black-waxed, cold, with a slip of creased paper beneath it. Not for you. For the next one. But you will need it. He does not read the rest. He puts the page down very gently on the desk, beside the cold tea, and stands, and goes to the door, and climbs the black stair into the night, where the glass lies silent and golden under a sky that is the same sky, the same stars, the same stars he has always known, and where a thousand years of the dead murmur, and wait, and do not know that anyone is listening.
